title: Quantum Random Access Memory Implementation Using Photon-Photon Interaction in Rydberg Atomic Ensemble
abstract: Quantum random access memory (qRAM) is crucial for overcoming data-loading bottlenecks in quantum machine learning; however, current physical implementations face severe scalability constraints. Traditional fanout designs demand exponential decoherence-prone gates, while bucket-brigade schemes require highly error-prone active switches. Motivated by these limitations, we propose a scalable qRAM architecture that fundamentally replaces active nodes with phase-encoded quantum walkers. Our methodology maps a discrete-time quantum walk onto a cavity quantum electrodynamics framework utilizing an electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT)-based Rydberg atomic ensemble. Inside hollow-core waveguides, strong Rydberg dipole-dipole interactions and a solenoidal magnetic field create a robust routing operator. This operator imparts precise, polarization-dependent phase shifts, steering circularly polarized probe pulses to target memory cells. Our results demonstrate that operating within a strong control field regime suppresses emergent spatial attenuation, ensuring cumulative transmission probabilities for highly scaled memory addresses. Ultimately, this parallelized architecture successfully optimizes spatial resources to static gates and temporal complexity to an optimal logarithmic scale of $\mathcal{O}(n\log(n+m))$ by requiring $\mathcal{O}(n+m)$ physical walkers, establishing a practical, fault-tolerant hardware pathway for advanced quantum computation implementations.
summary: This paper proposes a scalable Quantum Random Access Memory (qRAM) architecture by implementing quantum random walks using a Rydberg atomic ensemble in a cavity QED setup. It overcomes the decoherence and scalability issues of prior designs by encoding information into polarization-dependent phase shifts. The resulting framework achieves an optimal time complexity of O(n log(n+m)), providing a practical hardware pathway for quantum computation.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the scalability limitations of Quantum Random Access Memory (qRAM) implementations, which suffer from decoherence in traditional gate-based or switch-based designs.
main_result: The authors propose a scalable qRAM architecture achieving an optimal temporal complexity of O(n log(n+m)) by encoding quantum information into phase-encoded quantum walkers.
method: The methodology maps a discrete-time quantum walk onto a cavity QED framework, utilizing a robust routing operator derived from Rydberg interactions to steer polarization-dependent phase shifts.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Rydberg atomic ensemble within hollow-core waveguides, operating under an Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) scheme. The model involves deriving and solving equations for the Dark State Polariton (DSP) field propagation.
key_observables: Opposite polarization-dependent phase shifts ($\pm \varphi$), cumulative transmission probabilities, and the overall time complexity $O(n \log(n+m))$ for $n$ addresses and $m$ data qubits.
important_parameters: Strong control field regime ($|\Omega|^2 \gg \delta_{1,2}, \delta_d, \alpha$), and the ability to suppress spatial attenuation ($\kappa'_l$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the strong control field regime to suppress spatial attenuation and uses approximations such as the adiabatic and second-order perturbation expansions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the EIT double-ladder scheme, the physical operation of the polarization-dependent routing operator, and plots confirming attenuation suppression and information preservation across scaled memory depths.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the physical platform (Rydberg/EIT), deriving the necessary operators ($\hat{\Psi}, \hat{H}, \hat{S}$), and then recursively applying these operators to model the full cycle: encoding (writing), querying (CNOT), and decoding (retrieval) across binary tree layers.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics because it leverages complex, controllable quantum phenomena—specifically Rydberg interactions and EIT—to solve a fundamental problem in quantum computation (qRAM scalability). The coupling of quantum optics to quantum information theory is a key area of overlap.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Double-ladder Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) scheme utilized within the Rydberg atomic ensemble.

FIG. 2. Routing operator’s physical operation inside the Rydberg cell, showing interactions between counterpropagating weak ingle-photon ”signal” and coherent ”walker” probe pulses centred at t = 0 around z = 0 and z = L. (a) and (b) show left ( |ψL⟩ ) and right (|ψR⟩) circularly polarized probes interacting with oppositely polarized signals, acquiring distinct linear (Zeeman shift) and nonlinear (D-D interaction) phases for routing.

FIG. 3. Depicting the Quantum Random Walk-based qRAM architecture, n+m walkers traverse parallelized binary tree layers of interconnected phase-dependent waveguides, accessing memory addresses via double-rail encoding. (a) Routing operator Ψ exploits phase differences, steering left-polarized ( |L⟩) and right-polarized ( |R⟩) walkers into red and blue phase-selective waveguides. (b) Inverse operator Ψ† enables deterministic retrieval. (c) The dual-rail signal mechanism.

FIG. 4. Maps transportation of the probe walkers navigating the binary tree from root (0, 0) to distinct memory locations (010, 100, 111). Input in left circular polarization |L⟩, walkers at node (w, l) are manipulated by modified Hadamard H(w, l) and routing Ψ(w, l) operators to steer superpositions. Shift operator S(w, l) concurrently encodes the address qubit. Panels (a)(c) and (d)-(f) show routing of address |0⟩A2 ⊗|0⟩A1 ⊗|0⟩A0 and data |0⟩D2 ⊗|0⟩D1 ⊗|0⟩D0 walkers, respectively. (Left (Right) circular polarization state probe |L⟩carrying waveguide color-coded as red (blue)).

FIG. 5. Details the qRAM querying phase using dual-rail CNOT operations. Target memory information acts as control bits x0, x1, and x2, modifying data walkers D0, D1, and D2 stored in waveguides (|L⟩). Successive CNOT gates copy target data superpositions. Panels (a)-(c) show quantum querying from locations (010), (100), (111), respectively.
